Findings

What we know about the Indus script

What 150 years of study have established, what is still argued over, and what our own tests add.

What is knownStill disputedOur findingsClosed routesReversedPublishing

01Known

What scholars agree on

A short script on small objects

The Indus civilisation flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE across what is now Pakistan and north-west India. Its cities included Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira. The first inscribed seal was published in 1875, and the cities themselves were excavated from the 1920s.

About 4,000 to 5,000 inscribed objects survive. Most are square stone stamp seals two to three centimetres across, usually with an animal below a line of signs. There are also clay sealings, small moulded tablets, copper tablets and marks on pottery.

The texts are very short. In Mahadevan’s 1977 concordance, a face averages under four signs. Four in five have five signs or fewer, and the longest has 17.

About 400 signs

Scholars count roughly 400 distinct signs, depending on how variants are grouped: Mahadevan lists 417, Parpola about 386. That is far too many for an alphabet or a pure syllabary, and too few for a script where every word has its own sign.

So most scholars expect a mixed, logo-syllabic system, like Sumerian cuneiform or Egyptian hieroglyphs, where some signs stand for words and others for sounds.

Read from right to left

Most texts run right to left. Seals were carved in mirror image so their impressions read correctly. Where a writer ran out of room, the signs crowd together at the left end. Groups of short vertical strokes are widely accepted as numbers.

Contact with Mesopotamia

Indus seals and beads turn up in Mesopotamia and around the Persian Gulf. Cuneiform texts of the same period mention trade with a land called Meluhha, which most scholars identify with the Indus region.

A few round seals in Indus style were made in the Gulf. None of these objects carries a translation.

Then it stopped

The script fell out of use as the cities declined after about 1900 BCE. No later script descends from it that we can recognise. Brahmi, the ancestor of most South Asian scripts, appears about 1,500 years later, and no link to it has been shown.

02Disputed

What is still argued over

No bilingual has been found

Egyptian hieroglyphs were read with the help of the Rosetta Stone, and Linear B with place names already known from Greek. Nothing of the kind exists for the Indus script. No object pairs Indus signs with a text in a readable script.

Which language?

The language is unknown. The most developed proposal is an early form of Dravidian, the family of Tamil and Telugu, argued by Asko Parpola and Iravatham Mahadevan. Others have proposed an Indo-Aryan language related to Sanskrit, a Munda language, or a language that has since vanished.

More than a hundred decipherments have been announced. None has been accepted by specialists.

Is it writing at all?

In 2004 Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel argued that the signs are emblems, not a record of speech. In 2009 Rajesh Rao and colleagues answered with statistics suggesting language-like structure. Critics replied that such statistics cannot tell writing from other sign systems.

Our own tests agree with the critics on that point: at this corpus size, the statistics cannot settle the question either way.

03Strength

How to read the labels

Solid
Held up on texts we never looked at while building the idea, and survived a second team trying to break it.
Likely
Held up on unseen texts, but the numbers are small, so it could still be luck.
Shaky
The general pattern is real. The details are barely supported.
Not yet tested
Spotted in the data, but not yet checked on unseen texts.
A measurement
A count or measurement, not a test of an idea.

Is it new?

New
We know of no earlier report of this.
Partly new
The general idea was known; part of the result is new.
Tests an old idea
Checks a reading or claim made by earlier scholars.
Known, rechecked
Already known; we re-tested it more strictly.

“q” is the chance of a false positive after correcting for all the tests in a family or in the whole project (Benjamini-Hochberg). “Held-out” means texts kept apart while the idea was built. None of these findings gives a sound or a meaning to any sign.

04Ours

What our tests add: eleven findings

Grouped by how sure we are, and tagged by whether it is new. None of them tells us what a sign says yet. Each has a technical version with the numbers and code.

Solid4

  1. The signs follow rules about order

    Known, rechecked

    Shuffle the signs of a text and we can usually tell which order is the real one. That only works if the order follows rules, like words in a sentence.

    Technical version

    Sign order is fixed, not just positional

    Knowing the signs of an unseen text, the real order can be picked out from all orderings of the same signs far more often than chance. It still works with the commonest signs removed. Codes such as weather reports and chess openings pass this test too, so it shows a fixed format, not necessarily a grammar. It still holds with half the texts read backwards.

    Earlier work: Known since Mahadevan’s 1977 concordance and measured by Rao et al. (2009) and Yadav et al. (2010). New here: a test on texts held back from the model.

    40% of 321 held-out runs vs 5.7% by chance; q ≈ 8e-72

    Code and results: structure redteam revalidation

  2. “Six” followed by “fish” is a set phrase

    Tests an old idea

    The six-stroke sign and the fish sign appear together far more than chance, like “New York”. A popular idea that “seven + fish” means “seven stars” has almost no support.

    Technical version

    Six followed by fish is a fixed expression

    The six-stroke sign followed by the fish behaves like one set phrase. The proposed ‘seven stars’ reading of seven plus fish has almost no support.

    Earlier work: Parpola read six + fish as “six stars”, the Pleiades, and seven + fish as “seven stars”. The pair is confirmed as a unit; the “seven stars” reading is not supported.

    held-out 7 of 10 vs 3% base rate; q ≈ 6e-8

    Code and results: language redteam

  3. Seals, tablets and pots each use different signs

    Partly new

    From the signs alone we can often tell what kind of object a text was on, the way you can tell a shop sign from a letter.

    Technical version

    Each kind of object has its own vocabulary

    Seals, tablets, copper tablets, rods and pottery each favour different signs, enough to tell them apart on unseen texts.

    Earlier work: Differences between seals and tablets were noted before in general terms. New here: a measured test on unseen texts, across five kinds of object.

    held-out AUC: copper 0.87, tablet 0.76, pottery 0.73, seal 0.72, sealing 0.67 (chance ceiling 0.55–0.61)

    Code and results: context redteam

  4. Texts that run left to right were written that way on purpose

    Known, rechecked

    Indus texts normally read from right to left. The few that run the other way are deliberate reversals, not mistakes by modern readers.

    Technical version

    Texts written left to right are true reversals

    The few texts that run left to right are written backwards on purpose, not misread. This depends on each text’s direction label being right; with 1 in 10 flipped, the result misses its bar. The second edition of the texts cannot confirm it: too few left-to-right lines read the same in both.

    Earlier work: Right-to-left reading was shown by Lal (1966), and the left-to-right exceptions were listed by Mahadevan (1977). New here: a check that they are true reversals.

    31 of 34 copy-free lines; q = 6e-6

    Code and results: structure redteam

Likely4

  1. Four small ticks move the fish sign to the end

    New

    A plain fish sign can sit anywhere in a text. Add four small ticks and it usually comes last, so the ticks change how the sign is used, a bit like a word ending.

    Technical version

    Corner ticks move the fish sign to the end of the text

    A fish with four small ticks closes a text far more often than a plain fish: a mark inside a sign that changes where the sign goes. It holds on complete single-line texts too (9 of 16 vs 2%).

    Earlier work: We know of no earlier report that the ticks change where the fish sign goes.

    final in 40 of 73 vs 26% expected (p = 1e-7); held-out 11 of 19 vs 7% for plain fish (p = 0.004; q = 0.03 within its family, 0.54 across all tests)

    Code and results: novel_methods redteam

  2. Round seals from the Gulf break the usual rules

    Partly new

    Small round seals in a Gulf style were used by traders around Bahrain. Their signs come in an order Indus writers rarely used, wherever the seal was found. It could be another language, a special kind of seal, or imitation writing.

    Technical version

    Round Gulf-type seals break normal sign order, wherever they were found

    Round seals of the Gulf type, found abroad or at home, do not follow the usual sign order. This fits three readings our data cannot separate: another language, a round-seal genre in the Indus language, or pseudo-writing. They also rarely end with the usual closing sign (14% against about half of square seals). That different layout explains a third to a half of the odd order, not all of it.

    Earlier work: Parpola and others suggested that Gulf seals carry unusual sign sequences, perhaps in another language. New here: round seals found in Indus cities break the order too.

    order excess +1.64 bits/sign on 8 home round seals (Holm p = 3e-4, rare-sign-matched null); foreign vs home round +0.11 (p = 0.66)

    Corrected on 17 Nov 2026: a label error had hidden the home round seals. Only 3 of the 8 are confirmed round in a printed excavation report.

    Code and results: round_label_audit redteam_round_format redteam_round_order

  3. The middle of a seal text is just one or two signs

    Partly new

    Many seal texts have a fixed opening and closing. The part in between is usually one or two word-signs, not a name spelled out sound by sound.

    Technical version

    The core of a seal text is one or two signs, not a spelled-out name

    The part of a seal text between its fixed opening and closing signs is short and made of whole words, not spelled out sound by sound. Nothing shows these cores are names. This is the finding most sensitive to misread signs: at the real error rate between the two editions it fails in some simulated runs.

    Earlier work: Fixed opening and closing signs were known (Mahadevan 1977). New here: showing the part between them is usually one or two word-signs.

    34% of cores are one sign; recurring pairs keep one order in 91% of uses (held-out 115 of 138, p = 3e-16)

    Code and results: typology core_semantics

  4. The fish signs are variants of one sign

    Tests an old idea

    Six fish-like signs replace each other in the same places and pair with the same neighbours. They behave like forms of one word, not like names of six different gods.

    Technical version

    The fish signs form one class that substitute for each other

    Six fish signs swap for each other, combine with each other and share partners. The idea that fish signs are god names is not supported.

    Earlier work: Parpola grouped the fish signs and read them as star or god names. Our test supports the grouping but not the god-name reading.

    held-out p = 0.0002–0.0004

    Code and results: core_semantics

Shaky1

  1. Texts seem to have slots, like a sentence

    Known, rechecked

    Most texts fit a pattern of a few positions, such as an opening, a middle and a closing part. That positions exist is solid. Our exact list of them is not.

    Technical version

    Texts can be parsed into a small set of roles

    An 11-role reading parses most unseen texts, far more than shuffled ones. That positional roles exist is solid; that these 11 are the right ones is not. Role names such as ‘title’ and ‘noun’ are labels for positions, not tested meanings.

    Earlier work: Splitting texts into recurring parts goes back to Koskenniemi (1981), Parpola and Mahadevan. Our specific set of slots is new and weakly supported.

    parses 76% of unseen texts vs 44% for shuffles; specific roles p = 0.013, q = 0.085

    Code and results: functional_reading grammar

Not yet tested1

  1. Copper tablets repeat a few dozen fixed messages

    Known, rechecked

    Small copper tablets carry the same text-and-picture pairs again and again, like a set of standard tokens. We spotted this in the data but have not yet tested it on unseen texts.

    Technical version

    Copper tablets come in a few dozen fixed types

    Copper tablets repeat about 18 to 64 fixed text-and-picture types. A one-sign face can stand in for the picture, but the sign does not depict it.

    Earlier work: Copper tablets with repeated texts and matching animals were described by Parpola and others. Our type count is new but not yet tested.

    same legend → same sign face 8 of 8 (p = 1e-4, all data); blind matching 5 of 24 vs 3.3 by chance

    Code and results: context logograms

A measurement1

  1. About 400 signs: too many for an alphabet

    Known, rechecked

    An alphabet needs around 30 signs and a syllable script around 90. With about 400, most signs probably stand for whole words, as in early Chinese or Sumerian writing.

    Technical version

    About 400 signs: if this is writing, mostly word-signs, perhaps with sound-signs

    The sign count and how often each sign is used look like Proto-Elamite or Sumerian, not like Linear B or an alphabet.

    Earlier work: Mahadevan (1977) listed 417 signs and Parpola (1994) about 386. Both called the script mostly word-signs with some sound-signs.

    ≈400 signs (≈565 with unseen ones; 95% CI 508–658); 120 signs cover 90% of uses (Linear B: 63, Latin: 14)

    Code and results: structure

06Reversed

36 of our own results that the red team broke

These looked positive and did not survive an independent attack. They show where the traps are.

Show all 36
  1. v1 split leakage. 45% of held-out texts had a near copy in dev. Order prediction fell from 63% to 40.2% (vs 5.7% chance) on the clean split.
  2. Dholavira regional. 0.71 vs 1.19 became “not regional” once the comparison sites were added.
  3. Left-to-right direction. 134/150 became 31/34 on copy-free lines. Jar 33 vs 3 became 5 vs 0 (p = 0.03, q = 0.18).
  4. 7+fish. p 0.0025, then 0.017, then 0.07 on seals.
  5. M99 seal-specific. q = 1e-6 became 1.08×, p = 0.07.
  6. Rod register. 9 vs 0.5 became 6 vs 0.34, Mohenjo-daro only.
  7. Copper picture. 272 pairs became 18 legends. Sign level 0.485 became 0.030.
  8. Template test. 67% vs 25% was circular.
  9. Functional-reading lexicon null. q = 0.085.
  10. 3+fish. Failed held-out (2/22).
  11. Counted items. Code bug in `ll_spike`.
  12. Long texts. Rigged null.
  13. Number-names. M59 gives 15/16 hits.
  14. Rank signs. M336 is a W706 carving variant. M249 weakened. Zebu +42% became +11% (split luck).
  15. CONN = dumu. Built into the grammar; 0/48 grammar-free.
  16. naming_sim outlier. Construct-dependent.
  17. half_life P3. Family-driven.
  18. 1+12 numeral. Came from 3 families.
  19. Allograph perplexity. z −3.6 became p = 0.67.
  20. Typology spec A. IA 30/30 and NONLING 30/30 from the same machinery.
  21. Malayalam reads Sanskrit. 36% through loanwords.
  22. M99|M402 homophone. Did not replicate.
  23. M12 ligature. Below the bigram null.
  24. paragorth AAB repeats. p = 0.023; did not replicate in Wells.
  25. shaunmortal F23. Retracted.
  26. tamil-full-80. Also “passed” on planted Sanskrit and English.
  27. Cross-site short formula layer (identifiers S3). 145 objects on repeated 1-3 sign texts vs 151 expected under a bigram null; 0.89 vs 0.18 locality contrast was a length artefact (equal length: 0.51 vs 0.53).
  28. Seal cores more novel than personal names (identifiers). Ur III cores built the same way are more novel (0.96-0.995 vs 0.91-0.92); survives only against single names.
  29. No identifier repulsion as evidence against identifiers. Power 0.03-0.07 among contemporaries; real Ur III identifiers cluster.
  30. Repeated 4+ sign texts are re-cut seals of one holder, local like Ur III (red-team reading). Withdrawn by local_repeats: 43% same-site pairs vs 45% random; the 0.18 came from small reference sites.
  31. Numeral formula as a new find; “other 20 objects exceed chance” (local_repeats). The formula is the known M162 count frame (Wells W390 lumps five signs); the residual is 20 vs 18.6 expected under a fair null (p = 0.42).
  32. “Texts grow, never shrink” (local_repeats). p = 9e-9 shrank to 6 vs 1.8 expected (p = 0.005 trigram; 0.07 bigram); the singleton comparison measured commonness.
  33. Graded omission order on small seals (space_and_sealing T4, reg_size). Closer slopes equal a keep-one-closer random-deletion null (−0.0212 vs −0.0212); only “about one closer per text” stands.
  34. reg_size “new” seals. 41 of 138 were T4 seals counted twice (register-ICIT link gap).
  35. Ticked fish cluster by block (reg_findspot F3). Weakened: q = 0.114 over all 163 tests; not replicated elsewhere at Mohenjo-daro (p = 0.31).
  36. Connective M99 dropped first on small seals (T4). Did not replicate on register seals (+0.002, p = 0.41); not significant against the keep-closers null.

07Outputs

What can be published along the way

None of this needs a decipherment. Clean negatives and tools are worth publishing on their own.

  • A fair test bench for Indus sound keys Ready to write

    Paper and code. Five published readings, including the 185-sign key from 2026, score no better than their own values shuffled. The bench and its planted checks can be released for any new claim.

  • Round Gulf-type seals break Indus sign order, at home and abroad Needs one check

    Short paper. Passed two independent attacks. Before publishing, the shape of 5 of the 8 home seals needs checking, and a specialist should review the readings.

  • Structure of the script on unseen texts Ready to write

    Paper. Sign order predicted on held-out texts, the ticked fish that moves to the closing slot, and six plus fish as a fixed expression.

  • An atlas of closed routes Ready to write

    Open dataset. Over 80 tested routes, each with the size of effect its test could have caught, so nobody has to repeat them.

  • A small agent team with a shared task board Later

    Tool and write-up. The task board, the claim and red-team rules and the compute gate, as a reusable pattern for research with AI agents.
